10269: How do the biblical covenants fit together, and what is the relationship between ethnic Israel and the church of Jesus Christ?
10270:
Every reader of the Bible has to decide how the promises made to Abraham, Moses and David relate to the community gathered around Jesus. Are Israel and the church two stages of one people under one covenant of grace? Two distinct peoples with distinct promises? Or is the new covenant genuinely new, fulfilling and transforming everything before it?

The answer shapes how Christians read prophecy, apply the Mosaic law, baptize, and think about the modern Jewish people and the land. This entry sets out three families of answers at equal depth: covenant theology, dispensationalism (including its progressive form), and new covenant theology together with its close cousin progressive covenantalism.
10272:
Covenant theology reads the whole Bible through a small number of overarching covenants. Most Reformed versions speak of a covenant of works made with Adam, broken in the fall, and a single covenant of grace announced in Gen 3:15 and administered in different ways under Abraham, Moses, David and finally Christ. Many add an eternal covenant of redemption between the Father and the Son.

On this view there is one people of God across both Testaments. Believing Israel was the church in its childhood; the church today is Israel come of age, with Gentiles grafted into the same olive tree. Promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ, the true Seed, and in all who are united to him by faith. Many covenant theologians nonetheless expect a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ from Rom 11.

10318:
Dispensationalism holds that God has two distinct peoples with distinct (though related) purposes: Israel, an ethnic and national people with earthly promises of land, nation and Davidic kingdom, and the church, the body of Christ formed at Pentecost. History unfolds through a series of dispensations, stewardships in which God tests humanity under different arrangements.

Classic dispensationalists read prophecy with a consistently literal hermeneutic. Since God's promises to Israel were unconditional, they must be fulfilled to national Israel, most fully in a future millennial kingdom after the rapture of the church. Progressive dispensationalism, associated with Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock from the 1980s–90s, keeps the future for national Israel but sees the Davidic kingdom as already inaugurated in Christ and the church as a genuine (not parenthetical) stage in the one plan of redemption.

10366:
New covenant theology (NCT) and progressive covenantalism are mediating positions that arose largely among Reformed Baptists. They reject the dispensational two-peoples scheme, affirming one people of God fulfilled in Christ, but they also reject covenant theology's single covenant of grace with multiple administrations. Instead they trace a series of biblical covenants (Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, new) that progressively unfold and reach their goal in the new covenant.

The new covenant is genuinely new: all its members are regenerate, the Spirit indwells every member, and the law of Christ rather than the Mosaic covenant as a whole is the believer's rule, with the Decalogue binding only as taken up and reinterpreted in Christ. Israel functions as a type of Christ, the true Israel; the church is not Israel renewed nor a parenthesis, but the eschatological people formed in him. Progressive covenantalism, articulated by Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum, adds a stronger creation-covenant foundation and careful typological method.
